stem: What shape are the magnetic field lines around a long, straight wire carrying a current?

options.content: Circles centred on the wire
Straight lines parallel to the wire
Straight lines pointing away from the wire
The same shape as around a bar magnet

explanation: The field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles centred on the wire.

stem: A vertical wire carries a current downwards. Looking down on it from above (so the current flows away from you), which way do the field lines go round the wire?

options.content: Clockwise
options.rationale: Correct: thumb pointing away from you, fingers curl clockwise.

options.content: Anticlockwise
options.rationale: That is for a current coming towards you.

options.content: There is no field.
options.rationale: Every current has a magnetic field.

options.content: Up and down along the wire
options.rationale: The field lines circle the wire.

explanation: By the right-hand grip rule, with the thumb pointing along the current (away from you), the fingers curl clockwise.

stem: Reversing the current in a wire reverses the direction of its magnetic field.
explanation: The field direction depends on the current direction (right-hand grip rule).

stem: How does the strength of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire change with distance from the wire?

options.content: It increases further from the wire.
options.rationale: The field is strongest close to the wire.

options.content: It is the same at all distances.
It decreases further from the wire.
It is zero close to the wire.
options.rationale: It is strongest close to the wire.

explanation: The field is strongest near the wire, so the circles are drawn further apart as the distance increases.

stem: What does the magnetic field outside a current-carrying solenoid look like?

options.content: Circles around the solenoid
Like the field of a bar magnet
Uniform everywhere
options.rationale: The field is uniform only inside.

options.content: There is no field outside.

explanation: A solenoid's field is like a bar magnet's outside, and strong and nearly uniform inside.

stem: Looking at one end of a solenoid, you see the current flowing clockwise around the turns. Which magnetic pole is at that end?

options.content: A north pole
options.rationale: Anticlockwise current gives a north pole.

options.content: A south pole
No pole
options.rationale: Each end of a solenoid is a pole.

options.content: Both poles

explanation: Clockwise current (seen from the end) gives a south pole; anticlockwise gives a north pole.
hints: Use the right-hand grip rule: fingers along the current, thumb points to the north pole.

stem: Select **all** the changes that make an electromagnet stronger.

options.content: Replacing the soft-iron core with a copper core
options.rationale: Copper is not magnetic: the magnet is weaker.

options.content: Increasing the current
Putting a soft-iron core inside the coil
Reducing the number of turns
Reversing the direction of the current
Adding more turns of wire

explanation: More current, more turns and a soft-iron core all strengthen an electromagnet.
hints: Reversing the current changes the direction, not the strength.

stem: The current in a solenoid is doubled. What happens to the magnetic field inside it?

options.content: It becomes weaker.
options.rationale: A larger current gives a stronger field.

options.content: It reverses direction.
options.rationale: Only reversing the current does that.

options.content: It becomes stronger.
It does not change.

explanation: The strength of the field increases with the size of the current.

stem: In a relay, what does the current in the coil do?

options.content: It heats a bimetallic strip that bends and closes the contacts in the other circuit.
It flows directly through the second circuit as well.
It charges a capacitor that switches the second circuit.
options.rationale: A relay uses an electromagnet, not a capacitor.

options.content: It magnetises a core, which pulls an armature to switch other contacts.

explanation: A relay uses the magnetic effect of a small coil current to operate a switch in another circuit.

stem: Why does the cone of a loudspeaker vibrate?

options.content: The permanent magnet vibrates on its own whenever the signal current flows in the coil.
Sound waves travel down the wire into the cone.
options.rationale: The wire carries an electrical signal.

options.content: Static charge on the cone attracts and repels it.
The coil's changing current makes it push to and fro against the magnet.

explanation: The current in the coil, sitting in the magnet's field, feels a force that reverses as the current reverses, so the coil and cone vibrate.
hints: The coil carries a current and sits in a magnetic field.

stem: Match each arrangement with its magnetic field pattern.

right.content: Like the field of a bar magnet

explanation: Straight wire: circles. Solenoid: bar-magnet pattern outside, uniform field inside.

stem: What name is given to a long coil of wire that produces a field like a bar magnet when a current flows through it?
explanation: A long coil of wire is a solenoid.

stem: Complete the right-hand grip rule for a straight wire.

payload.template: The thumb points along the {{blank:a}} and the fingers curl in the direction of the {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Thumb: conventional current. Fingers: magnetic field lines.

stem: A learner investigates the magnetic field around a straight wire carrying a current.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe how the learner could show the shape and direction of the field.

points.description: Pass the wire vertically through a horizontal card and connect it to a supply that gives a large current
Sprinkle iron filings on the card and tap it gently: they form circles around the wire
Place plotting compasses around the wire to show the direction of the field (and reverse the current to see them turn round)

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Why must the current be large?

options.content: To heat the wire so the filings stick
options.rationale: Heating is a side effect, not the aim.

options.content: So the field is strong enough to move the filings
To make the field uniform at all distances around the wire
To reverse the field every few seconds
options.rationale: A steady d.c. current gives a steady field.

parts.explanation: The field of a straight wire is weak, so a large current is needed to see the pattern.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Seen from above, the compasses point clockwise around the wire. In which direction is the current?

options.content: Upwards, towards the viewer
Horizontally
It cannot be found.
Downwards, away from the viewer

parts.explanation: A clockwise field seen from above means the thumb, and so the current, points away from the viewer: downwards.

explanation: Iron filings show the circular pattern; compasses show the direction, which the grip rule links to the current.
hints: Use the right-hand grip rule backwards to find the current.
